title: Demonstrate an understanding of entrepreneurship and develop entrepreneurial qualities

lessons.title: What is an entrepreneur?
lessons.html:
What is an entrepreneur?

An entrepreneur is a person who sees a need and starts a business to meet it. The person takes a risk with their own money, time and work. If the business does well, they earn a profit. If it does badly, they can lose money.

Many entrepreneurs in South Africa started small, near a farm or in a village. Here are some examples:

  • Thandi grows spinach in her backyard and sells bunches at the taxi rank.
  • Sipho buys a second-hand bakkie and moves feed and fertiliser for small farmers.
  • Johannes keeps 50 layer hens and sells eggs to the spaza shop.
  • A group of farm workers start a stokvel and later buy a brush cutter to clear verges for money.

Employee or entrepreneur?

An employee works for someone else and gets a wage at the end of the week or month. An entrepreneur works for themselves. Nobody pays them a fixed wage. Their income comes from what customers pay, minus the costs of running the business.

EmployeeEntrepreneur
Gets a fixed wageEarns profit, which can go up or down
The boss carries the riskCarries the risk
Follows the plan of the businessMakes the plan and the decisions

Why entrepreneurs matter

Small businesses create jobs. When Sipho gets more transport work, he may hire a helper. Money then stays in the community. Small farm businesses also bring fresh food closer to people, so they do not need to travel far to the town.

You do not need a lot of money to start. Many good businesses start with a skill you already have, such as growing vegetables, fixing fences or looking after animals. You can start on weekends while you still have a job.

lessons.title: Qualities of a good entrepreneur
lessons.html:
Qualities of a good entrepreneur

People who do well in business usually share some qualities. You are not born with all of them. You can learn and practise them every day, at work and at home.

  • Hard work: a business needs long hours, especially at the start. Chickens must be fed on Sunday too.
  • Taking a sensible risk: start small, test the idea, and do not borrow more than you can pay back.
  • Creativity: look for new ways to solve a problem, for example selling vegetables in small packs that people can afford.
  • Confidence: believe in your product and talk to customers about it.
  • Honesty: sell good quality, give the right change and keep promises. Customers come back when they trust you.
  • Not giving up: hail may destroy a crop or a buyer may not pay. A good entrepreneur learns from the problem and tries again.
  • Planning: think ahead about money, seed, feed and transport.

How to build these qualities

  1. Set a small goal each week and check if you reached it.
  2. Keep a notebook of what you spend and what you earn.
  3. Talk to people who run businesses and ask what they learned.
  4. Do your job well at the farm. Being on time and reliable is good practice for running your own business.
  5. When something goes wrong, write down what happened and what you will do differently.

Example

Nomsa sold eggs but her hens stopped laying in winter. She did not give up. She asked the extension officer, fixed the feed and added light in the hen house. Her eggs came back and she kept her customers because she told them honestly what was happening.

Key points

  • An entrepreneur starts a business, carries the risk and earns profit.
  • Employees get a fixed wage; entrepreneurs do not.
  • Good entrepreneurs work hard, plan, are honest and do not give up.
  • Start small and take only sensible risks.
  • These qualities can be learned and practised every day.
